aliases: Tong Tian Xiang Jiang Hua Xiang
cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Jiang Hua Xiang type
processing: Classic dancong processing: sun-withering, firm overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, strip rolling and a light-to-medium charcoal roast in two or three passes with rests between them.
harvest_season: One spring picking, usually late April or early May.
appearance_dry: Long, heavy, dark brown strips with an intense spicy-floral smell.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, leathery olive leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: Ginger-lily spice and honey at full volume, a thick, oily body with ripe fruit, and a mountain-rhyme mineral finish that cools the throat for minutes.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps, soft water. Drink it on its own, not after a perfumed tea, and keep going past the sixth steep: the aftertaste is the reason for the price.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, ideally with the garden named, released in autumn after two or three roasts and rests, and often held a year before sale; it keeps three to five years sealed and dry. Top lots are made in small amounts, and the name is also applied to ordinary Jiang Hua Xiang.
description:
Tong Tian Xiang, the fragrance that reaches heaven, is a spicy, honeyed Phoenix dancong of the ginger-flower (Jiang Hua Xiang) type. Some sources use the two names for the same thing; others keep Tong Tian Xiang for a small, prized variety within the type.

Sellers speak of an old tree behind the name, and the name itself is said to describe a scent that carries, but neither the tree's age nor its site is firmly documented, and the often repeated claim that all Jiang Hua Xiang descends from it should be treated as trade lore.

The making is the patient dancong method: a firm overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, which brings out the spice, strip rolling and a light-to-medium charcoal roast done in two or three passes over the summer with rests in between.

In the cup it is Jiang Hua Xiang with the volume up: ginger-lily and white-flower spice, honey, ripe fruit, a thick oily texture, and in good lots a long, cold mineral aftertaste called shan yun. Brew it hot, fast and with soft water, and never after a loud tea.

It is sold by year, usually in autumn or the following year. The name is borrowed freely for ordinary Jiang Hua Xiang, so buy from an established Chaozhou seller, start with a small sample, and compare it with their high-mountain Jiang Hua Xiang: if the difference in depth and length is not obvious, you are paying for the story.
history:
Tong Tian Xiang, fragrance reaching heaven, is tied closely to the ginger-flower aroma of Phoenix dancong. Some accounts use it simply as another name for Jiang Hua Xiang, while others treat it as a small, prized variety within that type, with a clearer ginger edge than ordinary lots.

Little is documented beyond that. Sellers speak of an old Tong Tian Xiang tree, but no age, site or dated history for it could be traced to a firm record, and this is a tea whose story rests mostly on trade talk.
